newsitem.title: USA: Clinton spymaster nominee has golden credentials.
newsitem.headline: Clinton spymaster nominee has golden credentials.

text.p: George Tenet, President Bill Clinton's new choice to head the CIA, has risen smoothly through staff ranks in Congress and the White House to become acting director of the U.S. intelligence community.

Unlike Anthony Lake, who withdrew his name from consideration on Monday, Tenet was expected to win relatively speedy Senate confirmation because he is not closely linked with any controversial Clinton policies and because he once served as the Senate Intelligence Committee's staff director.
That is the committee with jurisdiction over this nomination and the one that begins the confirmation process.

"I have a lot of respect" for Tenet, Senate Intelligence Committee Chairman Richard Shelby, an Alabama Republican, said after Lake threw in the towel and condemned the confirmation process as "nasty and brutish without being short."
Shelby was Lake's chief antagonist, questioning his fitness to manage the sprawling U.S. spy community, and his regard is a valuable political asset for Tenet.

The new nominee has other advantages, too, having gone through vetting and confirmation for an earlier appointment as deputy CIA director and having served as acting director since last December pending the expected confirmation of Lake.
Tenet, 44, worked at the White House from 1993 until 1995 as chief intelligence adviser to Lake, Clinton's first-term national security adviser.

He coordinated all U.S. covert actions abroad while at the National Security Council, and crafted presidential directives on intelligence priorities, security coordination, spy-catching and satellite remote-sensing policies.

A sometimes gruff cigar-smoker said by colleagues to have a keen sense of humour, Tenet's Capitol Hill experience came as staff director on the Senate Intelligence Committee from 1988-93 under then-Chairman David Boren, an Oklahoma Democrat.

In that job Tenet pushed for tightened rules on the reporting of U.S. covert actions to Congress's intelligence panels in light of the 1986-87 Iran-contra affair, President Ronald Reagan's worst foreign policy fiasco in which White House aides secretly sold arms to Tehran and diverted profits to Nicaragua's contra rebels.
He became deputy director of central intelligence in July 1995 under then-Director John Deutch, who left in December after 20 months in the job, opening the slot for Lake.
Deutch was an enthusiastic Tenet backer, saying at his farewell appearance on Capitol Hill last year that he was confident of Tenet's ability to run the show in the interim.

If confirmed as director of central intelligence, Tenet would run the CIA and also oversee 12 other U.S. spy agencies that employ tens of thousands of people and spend about $30 billion a year overall.
He would be Clinton's third chief spymaster after Deutch and James Woolsey, who quit in December 1994 after becoming entangled in the case of convicted CIA turncoat Aldrich Ames.

The CIA has suffered a string of recent setbacks, from blown covert operations in friendly countries to disclosures about having taught torture techniques in Latin America in the early 1980s. Morale also been hurt by discovery of two Moscow spies in the ranks in recent years.
Associates said Tenet would be a popular choice with the CIA covert operations directorate, tarnished and shaken by the spy scandals. He has worked with the covert operations directorate for years.

He also has the requisite taste for deception that is the hallmark of a good CIA director, says former spymaster Woolsey, who once tried to recruit Tenet as general counsel for the Smithsonian Institution thinking he was a lawyer.
Tenet waited until he had polished off a fine meal at an Italian restaurant at Woolsey's expense before disclosing that he is not a lawyer, Woolsey recalled in an interview.

George J. Tenet was born January 5, 1953, in New York. He received a bachelor's degree from Georgetown University School of Foreign Service in 1976 and a master's from Columbia University School of International Affairs in 1978.
A resident of Potomac, Maryland, he is married to A. Stephanie Glakas-Tenet. They have one son, John Michael.
